opus-5.5.text:
I think what draws me to Lei Jun is that he's both a very strong engineer and someone who learned, over a long time, how to build an actual company. A lot of technical founders, myself included, start out believing that if the technology is good enough, everything else will follow. Lei Jun is a good counterexample. He was a legendary programmer early on at Kingsoft, but what he's really known for is understanding products, users, timing, and how to organize people around a mission.

One thing I really respect is his patience and persistence. Kingsoft was a long, grinding journey, and he went through many years where things weren't going the way he hoped. Then when he started Xiaomi, he was already around forty. That's encouraging to me, because it says entrepreneurship isn't only a game for twenty-year-olds who get lucky once. You can accumulate experience, reflect on your failures, and come back with a much clearer view of how the world works.

He also talks a lot about "standing on the wind," about finding the right trend. I think people sometimes misunderstand that as just being opportunistic, but to me it's about humility. Hard work alone isn't enough. You need to pick the right direction, and you have to be honest about whether the market really wants what you're building. As an engineer, that's a lesson I had to learn myself when moving from research to building Taichi as a company. Technical elegance matters, but whether it solves a real problem for real users matters more.

And finally, I like his focus on making good products accessible, with high quality but reasonable prices, and really caring about the user experience. There's a sincerity in that which I find inspiring. He's not someone who seems to just chase valuation; he seems to genuinely enjoy making things people use every day. That combination of engineering depth, long-term persistence, and user obsession is something I'd love to learn from.

r001.rationale: The response praises Lei Jun’s persistence but does not mention him missing the internet wave while focused on competing with Microsoft.

r002.rationale: It describes “standing on the wind” as choosing the right trend, but does not explain the flying pig theory as a trend propelling unlikely participants to success.

fable-5.1.text:
I think what draws me to Lei Jun is that he's one of the few founders who has built something very big twice, and did it the second time with a lot more self-awareness than the first.

With Kingsoft, he worked incredibly hard for years, and by his own account the results didn't match the effort. He was in his late thirties when he stepped back and asked himself a very honest question: why did someone who worked this hard not get the outcome he wanted? And his conclusion was basically that effort is necessary but it's not the thing that determines the outcome. Timing and direction matter more. That's where his famous line comes from, that you shouldn't fight the trend, you should ride it. For an engineer like me, that's a hard lesson, because engineers tend to believe that if you just build it well enough, things will work out. Lei Jun shows that you also have to pick the right wave.

The second thing is his approach to the product itself. Xiaomi started with a tiny team doing MIUI, releasing every week, and listening obsessively to a small group of users on a forum. That's a very startup mentality: iterate fast, stay close to users, let them shape the product. But he also combined it with a very clear business model from day one, which was keeping hardware margins thin and making the product so good at its price that it felt almost unfair. "Touching the price" people couldn't resist. Having both the product obsession and a sharp commercial model at the same time is rare.

The third thing, and maybe the one I personally admire most, is how he handles setbacks publicly. Xiaomi had very rough years around 2016 when the supply chain and sales collapsed, and he went in personally to fix it rather than hiding behind the org chart. He's also been willing to be a little uncool, to be laughed at for his English or for the "Are you OK" meme, and just keep going. There's a kind of durability there that I think is underrated. Founders talk a lot about vision, but the ability to stay in the game for twenty, thirty years through cycles is what actually compounds.

And now with cars, he's betting the company again in his fifties. You don't have to agree with every decision to see that this is someone who keeps learning and keeps putting himself on the line. That's what I want to learn from.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts Lei Jun’s hard work with the importance of timing and direction, but does not mention his focus on competing with Microsoft or missing the internet wave.

r002.rationale: It says to pick the right wave and ride the trend, but does not explain the flying pig theory’s point that a major trend can propel even unlikely participants to success.

astra-6.text:
What I find worth learning from Lei Jun is how he connects technology with what people actually want. As technical founders, we can get excited about building something sophisticated, but users care about whether it makes their lives better and whether they can afford it. Xiaomi is a useful example of taking those questions seriously.

I also admire the combination of ambition and attention to detail. You need a big vision, but you also need to get the product, the price, and the execution right. That balance is something I want to learn from.

What I find worth learning from Lei Jun is how he connects technology with what people actually want. Building a good product takes more than strong engineering—you also have to think about the experience, the price, and how you earn users’ trust.

I also admire the persistence involved in building a company like Xiaomi. As a technical founder, it’s easy to focus on the technology itself. His example reminds me to keep asking: Who are we building this for, and how can we make it valuable to more people?
